title: Ohio Truck Factory Layoffs Highlight a Region's Uneven Economic Change
summary:
Nearly 1,400 workers were laid off on Wednesday, September 30, at a Springfield, Ohio, truck factory formerly known as Navistar. The job losses were large enough to roughly erase an entire year's employment growth in the greater Dayton area, according to the report.

The layoffs affected families. Worker Kyle Bos, who has two daughters and another child due in January, described rising grocery costs alongside losing his job. Bos, a United Auto Workers member, said he planned to campaign for Democrats before November's election. He had voted for President Donald Trump three times but said he was done supporting him.

The layoffs came three days before Trump's Saturday rally at a nearby high school. Trump has been arguing that the economy is stronger than many voters believe. At a Texas truck plant on Thursday, he said manufacturing was returning and blamed poor public relations for negative views of the economy.

Dayton's industrial history helps explain why factory employment matters locally. The Wright brothers' airplane, the cash register, the stepladder and the electric car starter were all invented in the city. Yet federal data show that the surrounding area has lost about half of the 90,000 factory jobs it had in 1990.

The report describes production shifting to places where auto parts could be made more cheaply, with the trend accelerating after China joined the World Trade Organization. The region's economy has since developed other sources of employment.

Wright-Patterson Air Force Base has expanded and directly employs 38,000 people. Innovations associated with the base have attracted aerospace businesses, including Joby Aviation, Sierra Nevada Corporation and Electra. Aerospace businesses work on aircraft and related technology.

The White House cited Electra's $850 million investment and announcements from Honda, Stellantis and other companies as evidence that Trump's policies were creating jobs. Jeff Hoagland, who leads the Dayton Development Coalition, said the region's recovery reflected recognition by both Republicans and Democrats of Wright-Patterson's value over two decades.

Hoagland emphasized that economic development takes time. The layoffs and new investments show how different parts of one region's economy can move in different directions.
why_it_matters: The story connects family income, regional employment and election choices. It shows how factory job losses and investment in other industries can occur in the same region.
